Woollen
wul'-len
adj. (made of wool; in the law, one of the two fibres that might not be mingled in a garment)
From wool, Saxon wull. In the law of Moses woollen is always named beside linen, and the pairing is the point: an animal fibre and a vegetable fibre, which Israel was forbidden to weave into one cloth.

Biblical Definition

“Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together” (Deu 22:11), and in Leviticus among the statutes of separation: “neither shall a garment mingled of linen and woollen come upon thee” (Lev 19:19), set beside not letting cattle gender with a diverse kind and not sowing a field with mingled seed. These are the boundary statutes. They taught a people, by the clothes on their backs and the seed in their fields, that God had separated them and that holiness has edges. Notably the priests' garments and the tabernacle hangings did combine the fibres — the mixture was reserved to the sanctuary and forbidden to the common Israelite, which sharpened rather than blurred the lesson. The other four occurrences are the law of the fretting leprosy in a garment: “The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment” (Lev 13:47), examined in the warp or the woof, shut up seven days, and if the plague spread, “He shall therefore burn that garment… for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire” (Lev 13:52). A plague that could live in cloth had to be burned, not laundered. The ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ and no longer binds the conscience as to fibre; what abides is the doctrine it taught — that the holy and the common are not to be mingled thoughtlessly, and that some corruptions must be destroyed rather than managed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines woollen as made of wool, consisting of wool, pertaining to wool; and wool as the soft curled hair which grows on sheep and some other animals.

expand to see more

WOOLLEN, a. Made of wool; consisting of wool; as woollen cloth.

1. Pertaining to wool; as woollen manufactures.

WOOL, n. That soft species of hair which grows on sheep and some other animals, which in fineness sometimes approaches to fur.

LINEN, n. Cloth made of flax or hemp.

Key Scripture

Deu 22:11 — "Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together."

Lev 19:19 — "Ye shall keep my statutes. Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind: thou shalt not sow thy field with mingled seed: neither shall a garment mingled of linen and woollen come upon thee."

Lev 13:47 — "The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment;"

Lev 13:52 — "He shall therefore burn that garment, whether warp or woof, in woollen or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague is: for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire."

Modern Corruption

The mingled-fibre law is produced as proof that Scripture's moral commands may be discarded too; the threefold division of the law answers it.

expand to see more

Leviticus 19:19 is the favourite exhibit of those arguing that a Christian who eats shellfish and wears blended cloth has no standing to cite Leviticus 18 or 20 on sexual morality. The answer is not a dodge but the historic Reformed reading of the law, set out in LBCF 19: God gave Israel ceremonial laws, which prefigured Christ and are now abrogated; judicial laws, which expired with that state and bind only in their general equity; and the moral law, summarized in the ten commandments, which binds all men in all ages. The mingled garment is ceremonial — a visible schoolmaster teaching separation. The prohibitions of Leviticus 18 are moral, are grounded on the creation order rather than on Israel's calendar, are applied to the surrounding nations who had no ceremonial law at all, and are reaffirmed in the New Testament (Rom 1; 1Co 6:9-11).

The abiding principle in these statutes is real and should not be surrendered along with the fibre. God's people were taught holiness through their clothing, their fields and their herds, so that no part of ordinary life was outside the question of whether it belonged to Him. And the leprous garment adds a hard mercy: some things are not to be cleaned but burned. The Christian who keeps negotiating with a besetting sin, laundering it season after season, is refusing what Leviticus 13:52 says plainly — a fretting plague in the cloth means the cloth goes into the fire.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsemer (H6785), wool; pishteh (H6593), linen, flax; sha'atnez (H8162), a mixed fabric of wool and linen.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsemer (H6785) — wool; Leviticus 13:47-59, 19:19, Deuteronomy 22:11.

Hebrew pishteh (H6593) — flax, linen; always paired with wool in these statutes.

Hebrew sha'atnez (H8162) — a fabric of mixed stuff, wool and linen woven together; Leviticus 19:19, Deuteronomy 22:11 — the technical name for the forbidden cloth.

Hebrew kil'ayim (H3610) — two kinds, diverse kinds; the same statute's word for mingled seed and mixed breeding.

Hebrew mam'ereth (H3992) — fretting, malignant; Leviticus 13:52, a fretting leprosy that must be burnt.

Usage

"“A garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together” — forbidden to the common man."

"“Whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment” — the plague examined in the cloth."

"“It is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire” — not laundered."
